display_title: An interesting paper using paired samples to improve performance, but it still has a lot to improve.

content.title: An interesting paper using paired samples to improve performance, but it still has a lot to improve.
content.review:
Summary:
This paper works on the compositional question answering task on the DROP dataset. The authors present a framework that exploits paired questions to improve the learning of textual neural module network (Text-NMN). Specifically, the authors propose three ways to obtain paired questions in DROP: discovering paired questions within the dataset and generate paired questions based on templates or a question-generation model. The proposed model leverages the paired questions by minimizing the KL-divergence of the output distributions of the shared module in each pair. Experiments are conducted on a subset of the DROP dataset that is covered by the modules in Text-NMN and results show that the proposed model can improve both the in- and out-of-distribution generalization and leads to more accurate intermediate predictions with better faithfulness scores.

Strengths:
The proposed model leads to better answer accuracy and more accurate intermediate predictions compared to the baselines.

Questions:
1. I'm confused about the notations of Equation 5 (the learning objective) . What are the "g(q_i)" and "g(q_j)" here? In the above text, it states that "consider a question q_i that shares the substructure g(q) with a pair question q_j." Does g(q) denote a shared substructure or a probability distribution? In this case, isn't g(q_i) exactly equal to g(q_j) since they are shared by two questions? If so, why would the two distributions be different?

2. In Section 5, the numbers of found paired questions are reported. I think it would be better also to report the numbers in terms of each module, i.e., how many paired questions share a "find" module or a "filter" module? I think the "find" module would dominate the numbers since it often appears in the leaf nodes of the program tree and thus is more probable to be shared by two questions.

3. Are the ground-truth programs used for training? From the third paragraph of Section 3 ("Given a question q, ... the gold program z*"), it seems that the ground-truth programs are not used in training. However, in Section 4.1, the ground-truth programs are used to find paired questions and in Section 5, "We only use these program annotations for training"

4. Important training details are missing. For example, how is the learning objective (Eq.5) combined with the original loss function in Text-NMN?

5. The proposed method is dedicated to the compositional question answering task on the DROP dataset using neural module network and it is unclear how this proposed method can be generalized to other QA tasks. In this sense, it would be better to have a more accurate title than the current one, to avoid overclaiming too much.

6. The proposed method is highly related to enforcing the consistency of question-answering models and it would be better to discuss the related works on model consistency in the "Related Works" section, such as [1]. I am not an expert on this topic and there might many other related papers on model consistency.

[1] Are Red Roses Red? Evaluating Consistency of Question-Answering Models
content.rating: 4: Ok but not good enough - rejection
content.confidence: 4: The reviewer is confident but not absolutely certain that the evaluation is correct

display_title: Clarification about our approach, notation, and others

content.title: Clarification about our approach, notation, and others
content.comment:
Thank you for your review and finding our approach interesting. We provide clarifications and responses to the points raised above. Your response would help us update the paper to make it more clear.

1. Clarity in notation: For a given question ($x$), passage ($p$), and program ($z$), the modules in the program use BERT-contextualized question/passage representations as input. For example, given $x_1$ = “How many field goals were scored?”, and $z_1$ = count(find[“field goals”]), to execute find[“field goals”], the model is actually executing g(BERT($x_1$, $p$)[2:3]). Where, g=find, BERT($x_1$, $p$) is the contextualized representations for (question, passage) and the module gets as input the [2:3] slice denoting the representations corresponding to the 2nd through 3rd token of the question (“field goals”). We would like to introduce the notation ‘’g(BERT($x_1$, $p$)[2:3])’’ (in quotes) to denote the output of this execution (the distribution over passage tokens).  
Executing the same subtree for a different question $x_2$ = “How many yards longer was the longest field goal … “ would imply executing find(BERT($x_2$, $p$)[7:8]), which could lead to a different output since the input to the module is different due to contextualization, even though the surface form of the module input is the same. Prior work [1] has shown that in the presence of weak answer supervision, modules learn to behave in an unfaithful manner. An example of such behavior is also explained in “Complete example” (section 3) and empirically analyzed in Sec 5.4.  
Under this notation, sharing a substructure $g(q)$ implies that the paired examples share the subtree (e.g. $g(q_i)$ = $g(q_j)$ = find[“field goal”]) but their executions could lead to different outputs (as explained above). The consistency objective in Eq. 5 would encourage that the outputs of these subtrees, '’$g(q_i)$’’ and ‘’$g(q_j)$’’ (e.g. ''g(BERT($x_1$, $p$)[2:3])'' and ''g(BERT($x_2$, $p$)[7:8])''), are consistent. Equation 5 would now be:  
$L_{\text{paired}} =$ $- (KL[$‘’$g(q_i)$’’ $||$ ‘’$g(q_j)$’’$] + KL[$‘’$g(q_j)$’’ $||$ ‘’$g(q_i)$’’$])$.  
We can update our paper with this notation and discussion if it clarifies the confusion.  
[1] Subramanian et al. Obtaining Faithful Interpretations from Compositional Neural Networks. ACL 2020.

2. We will add these numbers in the paper. You are right, ‘find’ is much more frequently paired than ‘filter’.

3. We do use ground-truth programs while training, but also train the parser which is used to predict the programs during evaluation. 

4. We simply add the consistency objective (Eq 5.) with the original NMN loss. $L_{\text{final}} = L_{\text{NMN}} + L_{\text{paired}}$.

5. We discuss the point about wider applicability in a general response to the reviewers. [Scope of our approach](https://openreview.net/forum?id=mUU6jPGuvjx&noteId=zm4WcKux6-Q)

6. We do discuss our approach’s relation to work on enforcing consistency in QA models in section 2 (last paragraph) and the related work section, including mentioning [1]. It is worth noting that [1] and other prior work enforce consistency only at the level of the final answer and thus require labeled training data augmentation which is expensive to acquire. Our consistency objective on the other hand only requires that the paired examples (questions) share internal substructure, and hence does not require final (answer) supervision for augmented examples.
[1] Are Red Roses Red? Evaluating Consistency of Question-Answering Models

replying_to: Replying to Paired Examples as Indirect Supervision in Latent Decision Models
display_title: Concerns about the significance and applicability of the work

content.title: Concerns about the significance and applicability of the work
content.review:
This paper presents a method to leverage paired examples that share internal substructure and enforces the consistency between the internal representations. The solution is straightforward: (1) If two examples share a sub-module, then the probability distributions of the output modules should be similar, hence an auxiliary loss of KL divergence is added to the original training objective. (2) They also explored several ways to generate paired examples, either by leveraging existing examples from the training set or constructing them using templates or a question-generation model.  The approach is applied to the textual neural modular network (text-NMN) on a subset of the DROP dataset. The results show that 1) it improves over its own baseline marginally in in-distribution evaluation; 2) the model can obtain better faithfulness scores and achieve better performance in compositional generalization settings.

Overall, I am ambivalent about this paper. The paper is easy to read and well-written and the general direction (enforcing consistency of latent decisions leads to better compositional generalization) is appealing. On the other hand, I am concerned about the significance of this work: The approach is straightforward and not particularly new (this doesn’t have to be a major weakness though) and the results are evaluated on only one dataset with gold programs provided. I think it largely limits the applicability of the approach. It is also hard to evaluate the experimental results and put them in context (as there is really no prior work to compare to). I will elaborate on these points more below. 

As the paper puts, one major difference of this approach compared to prior work (e.g., Li et al 2019, Asai and Hajishirzi, 2020) is that this approach is operated at intermediate latent decisions whereas previous work only operated at outputs. However, this paper used gold program annotations to identify paired examples and to train the model. Why can’t we just think of gold programs as outputs then? I would be much more convinced if the gold programs are not used and some consistency losses can be still enforced on latent decisions. Also, when finding naturally paired examples, it is constrained to programs that share a leaf *find* module (similarly for the templates used in generating paired examples). I think these constraints are all too specific and tailored to one single dataset. 

It is also a bit difficult for me to interpret the experimental results.
- Table 1: is it a fair comparison to (Hu et al, 2019)? I believe their work didn’t use gold programs.  PS. In the Dev + EM column, 62.4 is higher than 61.6 should be written in bold.
- The evaluation of faithfulness scores is also somewhat surprising to me. The faithfulness score measures whether each module can be correctly aligned to the corresponding set of spans. Isn’t this information already provided as a training signal (in gold programs)? I am not sure why adding this pairwise auxiliary loss will help. Given that the gold program is used, how if you just add an auxiliary loss in addition to the final answer prediction so that it encourages the model to output correct sets of spans in every single module (no need to use paired examples)? I could have misunderstood something..

Finally, it would be really great if the approach can be evaluated in more datasets, and in the setting that no gold program is used. Otherwise, I think the general applicability of the approach is limited or unclear. 

Minor: 
- It took me a while to understand the notations in Figure 1. I think they need to be clarified, e.g., What does “g(x2,[13:13])” refer to?
- Similarly, explain what is “G.P.” in Table 3.
content.confidence: 3: The reviewer is fairly confident that the evaluation is correct

display_title: Gold programs do not contain module output supervision, and other clarifications

content.title: Gold programs do not contain module output supervision, and other clarifications
content.comment:
Thank you for your review. We appreciate that you found our approach appealing and our paper well-written. Below we provide clarifications and discussion to the points raised. Your response will help us provide an updated version of the paper to address your concerns.

We would first start with clarifying the notation. For a given question ($x$), passage ($p$), and program ($z$), the modules in the program use BERT-contextualized question/passage representations as input. For example, given $x$ = *How many field goals were scored?*, and $z$ = count(find[“field goals”]), to execute find[“field goals”], the model is actually executing g(BERT($x$, $p$)[2:3]). Where, g=find, BERT($x$, $p$) is the contextualized representations for (question, passage) and the module gets as input the [2:3] slice denoting the representations corresponding to the 2nd through 3rd token of the question (“field goals”). We would like to introduce the notation ‘’g(BERT($x$, $p$)[2:3])’’ (``in quotes) to denote the output of this execution (for example, the distribution over passage tokens). 

We would like to clarify that the gold programs only contain supervision for the layout of the modules and *not* the gold module outputs. In the example above, we are only provided with the fact that $z$ is count(find[“field goals”])) and not the gold passage spans that should be output by the find module (‘’find[“field goal”]’’).
The answer supervision (output of the root of the program tree) is a very weak training signal for what the outputs of the intermediate modules in the program should be (e.g. supervision = ”2” instead of indicating what passage spans are relevant). Our approach applies a consistency objective between the predicted outputs of the intermediate modules in paired examples’ program trees, thus providing an indirect supervision to the intermediate module outputs. For example, to the outputs ‘’g(BERT($x_1$, $p$)[2:3])’’ and ‘’g(BERT($x_2$, $p$)[7:8])’’ for paired examples $x_1$ and $x_2$ in Fig 1.  Our annotation is simply that $x_1$[2:3] corresponds to $x_2$[7:8], so the outputs of these two functions should be the same, whatever they may be.
You are correct in judging that in the presence of gold module output supervision, using our approach would be inconsequential. We do not have such supervision; it is very challenging to collect.  Using a consistency loss with paired examples gives a way of approaching that supervision without the corresponding annotation cost.


Comparison to MTMSN (Hu et al, 2019): We would like to reiterate from Sec. 5 (baselines) that the focus of our work is improving learning in structured interpretable models. We propose a consistency objective to provide indirect supervision to latent decisions, and measure its impact by using it with a NMN. We also provide results for a competitive black-box model (MTMSN) as reference to place the final model’s performance in context. We agree that the NMN uses extra supervision in terms of gold programs and future research is required to close this gap between black-box and structured interpretable models.

We discuss the point about general applicability in a common response to the reviewers. [Scope of our approach](https://openreview.net/forum?id=mUU6jPGuvjx&noteId=zm4WcKux6-Q)

content.title: Anonymous Review
content.review:
This paper studies latent decision model for language understanding and text question answering. This work introduces a new training objective that maximizes the consistency between pairwise samples that have similar latent structure. This work also proposes ways to acquire training data for the pairwise consistency objective. The proposed model is evaluated on the recent DROP dataset, achieving superior performances over itself without the pairwise objective, and a recent baseline MTMSN. The paper is very well written and the results are clearly presented.

There are a few things on which I would suggest further improvement and clarification:

1. The experiments impose strong condition on the dataset and model, and is only performed on a subset of the DROP dataset due to this reason. Given the claim made in this paper, it remains questionable how this model extends to boarder scenarios. 

2. It is unclear whether the improvement comes from more training data or a better objective. Are the baseline models leveraging the extra data that the authors gathered for consistency training? If not, then I will suggest further investigation under stricter benchmarking of the data usage. To my opinion, the current experiments are not sufficient enough for establishing the claims.

3. On a higher level, adding the consistency loss will inevitably require extra labels (or efforts to generate these labels). What is the advantage of baking the consistency relation into a learning based model rather than directly applying the mechanism that gives you these labels in the first place? For example, why not directly compare to BERT ; or why not impose the heuristics to directly solving the task. Any justifications?

Based on the above assessments, I suggest rejection of this paper. Even though I think this paper tackles a very important task from a promising direction, the current experimental evaluations need to be stronger to be more convincing.
content.rating: 4: Ok but not good enough - rejection

display_title: Clarifications about no new extra training data used

content.title: Clarifications about no new extra training data used
content.comment:
Thank you for your review. We appreciate that you found our paper well written, with clear empirical results.
Below we provide discussion to the points raised in the review and ask clarification questions that will help us revise the paper to make it clearer.

3: “adding the consistency loss will inevitably require extra labels” - We would like to clarify that using our proposed consistency loss does not require extra ($x$, $y$) pairs. Indeed, the third row in Table 1 (+$L_{\text{paired, found}}$) uses *exactly* the same ($x$, $y$) pairs as rows 1 and 2, it just uses them differently, with an additional paired loss function. The other rows in table 1 add new $x’$, but without any associated $y’$. We only supervise that certain pairs of questions share sub-structure and enforce consistency in the execution of the latent decision. This additional supervision signal cannot be used in unstructured black-box models.
In light of this clarification, could you please clarify what you meant by the following suggestions -- “directly applying the mechanism that gives you these labels”, “why not directly compare to BERT”, “why not impose the heuristics to directly solving the task”. 

2: As explained above, we do not provide more training data to the model. When the NMNs use _exactly_ the same ($x$, $y$) pairs, using our paired objective leads to improved performance; Table 1, row 3 vs 2 shows dev: $+3.4$ F1 and test: $+0.7$ F1 improvements. We see additional improvements on using new $x’$ (questions only) --- such data cannot be leveraged by a black-box model or even an NMN trained with standard loss functions. Can you explain the experiment you had in mind that would have stricter benchmarking of data usage?

1: We discuss extension to broader scenarios in a general response to all reviewers. [Scope of our approach](https://openreview.net/forum?id=mUU6jPGuvjx&noteId=zm4WcKux6-Q)

display_title: A decent work with a reasonable idea and solid experiments

content.title: A decent work with a reasonable idea and solid experiments
content.review:
This paper proposes to train NMTs with the self-supervision that the partial models with the shared structure should generate the same outputs. On the task of question answering, they explore three different ways to generate paired training examples with shared substructures and demonstrate all of them lead to improvement on both in- and out-of distribution test data on DROP dataset.

The main idea is reasonable and can be applied to many models in which the computation is dynamic and corresponds to some latent symbolic structures. The experiment results also validate the effectiveness of the proposed approach. The experiments of faithfulness and compositionally provide some intuition on how this pair loss could help the training of NMTs. 

In general, I think this is decent work without apparent disadvantages. 

===================================================================
After reading other reviewers' comments, I degrade my rating to 6 due to the concern of experiments and applicability.
content.confidence: 2: The reviewer is willing to defend the evaluation, but it is quite likely that the reviewer did not understand central parts of the paper

content.title: Scope of our approach
content.comment:
We propose a consistency objective that aims at providing indirect supervision to intermediate outputs in structured latent decision models by leveraging paired examples. Our proposed approach does not make any assumptions about the class of models it can be applied to, apart from the fact that the model produces interpretable latent outputs. Therefore, it is applicable to a wide variety of latent decisions models that the community is exploring for various tasks, including, but not limited to, language models with latent coreference, syntax, or entity-linking, weakly supervised semantic parsing, checklist-style models, etc.
The specifics of how to exactly apply the paired objective in different models is not trivial and our experiments provide strong evidence for its various merits on one popular approach for complex question answering.

Many approaches for complex NLP tasks have found that models fail to generalize when trained using weak supervision and resort to data augmentation as a solution. Data augmentation is performed in a task specific manner and is non-trivial in scenarios where acquiring end-task supervision ($y$) is challenging. Our paired objective on the other hand can be used by discovering paired examples within the dataset or augmenting new input examples ($x’$), without requiring the output supervision ($y’$) for them. 

In this work, we show that the indirect supervision provided by the paired objective leads to improved in-distribution performance and compositional-generalization to out-of-distribution examples. Importantly, we show that this indirect supervision helps the NMN learn correct module execution, i.e., correctly predict latent decisions, thus showing that the performance is improving for the right reasons. We would argue that our work provides sufficient evidence showcasing the efficacy of our approach and future research should explore how this approach can be applied to other tasks and models.
